Infantino's design work on the New Look, including the yellow-ringed emblem, modernised the character's appearance for the first time since 1939 and provided the visual basis for the 1966 television series.
Fox scripted Batgirl's introduction to a brief supplied by the television production: a competent, independent woman with her own reasons, rather than a female counterpart defined by the hero.
Infantino designed the costume and drew her first appearance, giving her a look that has survived essentially unchanged through every subsequent revision of the character.

Miller's premise — an ageing Batman returning to a Gotham of gang violence and saturation news — let him treat the character as a political problem rather than an adventure hero, ending with a state-sanctioned Superman sent to stop him.

Miller drew the series with Klaus Janson and Lynn Varley, using dense sixteen-panel grids and television screens as narration — a formal approach as deliberate as Watchmen's, and published in the same year.
Year One ran in the monthly Batman title rather than as a prestige miniseries, retelling Bruce Wayne's first year alongside Jim Gordon's arrival in a police force where honesty is the aberration.

The series recast Batman permanently as an obsessive and a potential authoritarian rather than a deputised crimefighter, and its commercial success made that reading the industry default for two decades.

Year One displaced every earlier account of the character's origin and supplied the structure — the failed first outing, the bat through the window, the corrupt police force — that later comics and films have followed almost without variation.

Published in prestige format at a premium price and sold successfully to adults through bookshops, it demonstrated that DC could operate outside the newsstand entirely, and helped establish the graphic novel as a retail category.

Snyder's five-year New 52 run with Greg Capullo built its central story around the Court of Owls, a secret society claiming to have governed Gotham for centuries — an argument that Batman had never understood his own city.

Lee's Batman: Hush with Jeph Loeb in 2002 was a deliberate commercial exercise, touring the character's entire rogues gallery, and it made him DC's marquee artist and eventually one of its senior executives.

The ABC series played the character as deadpan camp twice weekly and made him a global phenomenon within months. It also fixed a reputation for silliness in the public mind that DC's writers spent the following twenty years dismantling.

The producers wanted a new female lead for the third season, and DC introduced Batgirl in the comics first so that the character would arrive on screen with an existing history — an early instance of publishing serving screen requirements.

Burton's film drew directly on the darker comics of the preceding years and, with an unprecedented merchandising campaign, erased the camp association left by the television series in a single summer.

Miller's ageing, brutal Batman and Burton's gothic Gotham arrived within three years of each other, and the film's success is generally credited with confirming to Warner that the darker reading of the character was the commercially valuable one.
The animated series was commissioned in the wake of the film's success and inherited its art-deco Gotham and Danny Elfman's musical register, then quietly outdid it in writing and characterisation.

Timm and Radomski's series animated on black paper to make Gotham permanently nocturnal, treated the villains as tragedies, and through Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill's performances became the definitive version of the character for a generation.

Nolan's film placed the character in a plausible modern city and built its plot around institutional fragility rather than costumed spectacle, making the case that superhero films could be treated as serious cinema.

Heath Ledger's performance, drawing on the deliberately unfixed origin established in The Killing Joke, won a posthumous Academy Award and reset public expectations of what a comic book villain could be.

Harley Quinn was written for a single 1992 episode as a henchwoman with a Brooklyn accent, voiced by Arleen Sorkin. She became so popular that the comics adopted her — the clearest case at DC of an adaptation feeding a character back into the source.

Dini and Timm's Mad Love established her as an Arkham psychiatrist manipulated and abused by her patient. Later writers took the abuse seriously and had her leave him, which is what turned a sidekick into DC's most commercially successful modern character.

Marston proposed the character to Max Gaines after publicly defending comics in a magazine interview, arguing that the genre needed a hero who conquered by love rather than force. He wrote the strip as Charles Moulton until his death in 1947, drawn throughout by H. G. Peter.

Wonder Woman was introduced in a backup feature in All Star Comics #8 at the end of 1941, moved to the lead of Sensation Comics within a month, and had her own title by the following summer — an unusually fast promotion.

Gaines hired Marston as an educational consultant to give All-American academic cover against the era's critics, and then let him write the character he had proposed. It is the rare case of a publisher's public-relations hire producing a lasting creation.

Pérez's 1987 relaunch after Crisis restarted the character from her first arrival in the outside world and grounded her firmly in Greek myth, treating her as an emissary rather than a costumed adventurer. It is generally regarded as the modern foundation of the character.
Pérez drew as well as plotted the relaunch, designing a Themyscira of classical architecture and a cast of Amazons with individual faces — the visual vocabulary the character has used since.

Fox and Harry Lampert introduced the first Flash in 1940, giving him super-speed from hard water vapour and a winged helmet taken from his father's war service — an origin that reads as pulp science even by the standards of its own decade.

Finger scripted the first Green Lantern from Martin Nodell's concept: a railway engineer who survives a bridge collapse and forges a ring from a mystical lantern, its power arbitrarily useless against wood.

Fox devised the Justice Society for All Star Comics #3 as a way of showcasing several titles at once, giving each hero a solo chapter of a shared case. It was the first superhero team, and it invented the crossover as a commercial device.

The team assembled in All Star Comics #3, dated Winter 1940. The book's structure — a framing sequence, individual chapters, a shared conclusion — remained the standard team-comic format for two decades.

Garrick was a charter member, and by the rules of the day so successful that he was moved to honorary status to make room for less established heroes — a mechanism the writers used to keep the roster promoting weaker titles.
Scott was another founder, and his Golden Age partnership with Garrick became the model for the long friendship between the two men that later Justice Society writers made the team's emotional core.

Wonder Woman joined the Society shortly after her debut and was made its secretary, a detail frequently cited as evidence of how narrow the era's imagination was even about the character created to widen it.

The League was explicitly modelled on the Society, updated for a science-fiction age and a mass-market name. Julius Schwartz chose the word League over Society on the grounds that American readers knew baseball leagues better than learned societies.

Schwartz used Showcase as a laboratory: test a concept over a few issues, measure the sales, and promote only what worked. The Flash, Green Lantern, Adam Strange and the Challengers of the Unknown all reached print through it.

Showcase #4 in 1956 introduced a new Flash with a new name, job and origin, keeping only the concept. The decision to rebuild rather than revive is the single editorial choice from which the whole Silver Age follows.

Showcase #22 in 1959 repeated the Flash method on Green Lantern, replacing a magical Golden Age hero with a test pilot recruited by dying aliens into an interstellar police force — the shift from mysticism to space opera that defined DC's 1960s.

Infantino redesigned the Flash as a smooth red silhouette with no visible seams or belt, and drew speed as trailing multiple images rather than motion lines. The design has survived essentially unaltered for seventy years.

Broome wrote most of the character's formative years and built his rogues gallery — Captain Cold, Gorilla Grodd, Mirror Master, the Reverse-Flash — a set of recurring, non-lethal, personality-driven villains unusual for its coherence.

Broome scripted Green Lantern's introduction and invented the surrounding apparatus: the Guardians of the Universe, the Corps, the oath, and Sinestro as a fallen member of the hero's own police force.

Kane designed the crew-cut test pilot and the sleek green and black costume that replaced Alan Scott's ornate Golden Age outfit, and drew the character's first decade with the dynamic low-angle figure work he was known for.

Schwartz had been Broome's literary agent in science fiction before either worked in comics, and their long partnership gave the Silver Age its characteristic tone: brisk, rationalised adventure with a scientific alibi for everything.
Schwartz commissioned from Fox both the Justice League and Flash of Two Worlds, the two ideas that turned a set of revived characters into a connected universe with its own history.
Schwartz paired Infantino with the revivals and let him redesign as he went. The clean, modern look that resulted is as responsible for the Silver Age's success as any script decision.

Flash of Two Worlds in 1961 had Barry Allen vibrate onto a parallel Earth and meet the hero he had read about as a boy. The story created the multiverse, made DC's own back catalogue part of its fiction, and invented the legacy structure the company still runs on.

West took the identity after Allen's death in Crisis on Infinite Earths — the first time at DC that a sidekick permanently replaced his mentor in a flagship role, and the decision that made legacy succession a real principle rather than a temporary stunt.

The two Green Lanterns share little beyond a ring and a name: Scott's power is magical and personal, Jordan's is issued by an interstellar bureaucracy. The gap between them is the clearest single measure of what changed between the Golden and Silver Ages.

Stewart was introduced as Jordan's designated replacement, initially resented by him, and spent years as a substitute before becoming a lead Green Lantern in his own right and, through animation, the most widely recognised version of the character.

O'Neil wrote Stewart's introduction as a direct challenge to Jordan's assumptions — an architect who refuses to wear a mask because he has nothing to hide, and who is proved right about the story's racist antagonist while the hero is proved wrong.

Adams designed Stewart and drew his first appearance during the run in which he and O'Neil were deliberately testing whether a mainstream superhero comic could carry arguments about race without flinching.

O'Neil opened the run with a Black man asking Green Lantern why he has helped every colour of alien and never his own people, and gave the hero no answer. The stories that followed took the two heroes across America to argue about poverty, pollution, cults and addiction.

Adams drew the run with the naturalism he had brought to Batman, staging arguments in real American landscapes rather than generic cityscapes — the visual argument that these were not fantasy problems.

The run reframed Jordan permanently as an authority figure whose instincts require examination, a reading that later writers pushed to breaking point when they had him destroy the Corps and then spent a decade rehabilitating him.

Pairing a licensed cosmic policeman with a bankrupt left-wing populist gave the Bronze Age its most productive argument, and the friendship survived it: the two have been written as antagonistic allies ever since.

Weisinger and Paul Norris introduced Aquaman as a backup feature in 1941. He is one of very few Golden Age heroes to survive continuously into the Silver Age, when he acquired Atlantis, a throne and the political burden that later writers built him around.

Weisinger and George Papp built Green Arrow from the Batman formula with archery substituted for detection, complete with a sidekick, a signal arrow and an Arrowcar. It took thirty years and Neal Adams's redesign to make him distinctive.

Aquaman first appeared in More Fun Comics #73 in 1941, in the same issue as Green Arrow — an unusually productive month for a title that had begun life as the company's loss-making experiment in original material.
Green Arrow's debut shared More Fun Comics #73 with Aquaman's. Both were designed as reliable backup features rather than headline characters, and both outlasted almost every hero who was.

O'Neil bankrupted Oliver Queen, took away his gadgets and gave him a temper and a political argument, converting a second-string Batman imitation into the most explicitly left-wing voice in mainstream superhero comics.

Fox wrote the League's debut in The Brave and the Bold #28 in 1960 and its first several years, using a rotating cast and a standard structure of splitting the team into pairs against a single threat.

Superman was a founding member but was used sparingly in the early years, since editorial protected the flagship characters and a hero who could solve most plots alone is a structural problem for a team book.

Batman's presence in the League has always required justification — the one member without powers — and writers from Gardner Fox to Grant Morrison have made that anomaly the point, casting him as the team's strategist and its check on itself.

Wonder Woman's charter membership secured her place in DC's central trinity, the three characters treated as the company's permanent core regardless of how many times the surrounding continuity is rebuilt.
Allen was a founding member and, in most versions of the origin, the one who proposes the team — appropriate for the character whose own revival had started the era that made the League possible.
Jordan joined at the founding, bringing the interstellar scale of the Green Lantern Corps into a book that otherwise ran on Earth-bound threats and giving writers a route to cosmic plots.

Aquaman's charter membership kept him at the centre of DC's continuity through decades in which his solo titles sold poorly, and later writers used his kingship to make the League's dealings with Atlantis a diplomatic rather than heroic matter.

The Martian Manhunter has served in more rosters than any other member and is routinely written as the team's continuity and its conscience — the one who stays when the flagship characters leave for their own books.

Kirby came to DC in 1970 on the promise of writing, drawing and editing his own titles, and used the freedom to build an interlocking modern mythology about the war between free will and its abolition.

The Fourth World books contain some of the most extreme drawing of Kirby's career — collaged photographic textures, cosmic machinery, the crackling energy fields that bear his name — and were cancelled before he could finish the story.

Kirby designed Darkseid as the opposite of a flamboyant supervillain: immobile, patient, granite-faced, and interested only in the Anti-Life Equation, a formula that would end free will everywhere. He has since become DC's default cosmic threat.

Darkseid first appeared in a single panel of Superman's Pal, Jimmy Olsen #134 in December 1970 — a seated figure watching a monitor, unnamed and unexplained — and in full in The Forever People #1 two months later. Introducing the villain in a Superman spin-off before his own titles existed tied the Fourth World into the DC universe from the outset rather than leaving it as a separate imprint.

As DC's editorial director Infantino personally recruited Kirby away from Marvel, offering the creative control and ownership terms Kirby had been denied there. The commercial results disappointed both men; the creative legacy outlasted the company that cancelled it.

Kirby placed Darkseid opposite Superman deliberately, setting the character who represents the promise of power against the one who represents its appetite. The pairing became a fixture of the Superman titles and of nearly every animated adaptation.
Darkseid's invasion is the League's origin story in several continuities, including the New 52 and its screen adaptations — the threat large enough to require the founding of the team.

Wein wrote a standalone horror story for House of Secrets in 1971 about a man transformed into a plant creature by chemicals and betrayal. Reader response was strong enough that the character was given his own title within a year.

Wrightson's dense, gothic pen work established the character's Louisiana swamp register and remains the reference point for every artist who has drawn him since, despite Wrightson leaving the title after ten issues.

Moore inherited a title scheduled for cancellation and opened by revealing that the creature had never been a transformed man — only vegetable matter that had absorbed a dead man's memories and believed itself to be him. The revision made the character an elemental and the book a critical event.

Moore introduced Constantine with Stephen Bissette and John Totleben in 1985 as a working-class English occultist who manipulates the powerful and survives everyone around him. The artists had wanted to draw someone who looked like Sting; the character was built to fit.

Constantine appeared first as an unexplained figure who seemed to know more than the protagonist, a deliberate refusal to supply an origin. He was given his own title, Hellblazer, three years later; it ran for three hundred issues.

Berger recruited Moore to the title on the strength of his British work and then defended the run's departures from house practice, including the decision to publish without the Comics Code seal — the precedent on which Vertigo was later built.

Berger's recruitment of Moore began the British invasion of American comics, and her success with him gave her the standing to bring over Gaiman, Morrison, Delano and Milligan in the years that followed.

The run proved that a mature, Code-free, single-author horror comic could sell profitably through the direct market. Vertigo was essentially the institutionalisation of that discovery eight years later.

Constantine spent the Moore run steering Swamp Thing towards a destiny he refused to explain, using him as he uses everyone. The relationship set the pattern for how the character has been written for forty years.

Gaiman took a discarded Golden Age title name and wrote seventy-five issues about Dream of the Endless, structured as a single story about whether a being older than gods can change. He ended it deliberately in 1996 rather than let it continue without him.

Berger commissioned the series from a writer with almost no American track record and protected its unusual shape — anthology issues, rotating artists, an announced ending — against the commercial logic of monthly publishing.

Sandman predated Vertigo by four years and was folded into the imprint at its 1993 launch, where it became the commercial anchor: a comic that sold in bookshops, to adults, and in unusually large numbers to women.

The series supplied the imprint's argument to the trade: that literate, creator-driven, non-superhero comics could support a permanent line, and that collected editions could earn more over time than monthly issues.

Berger brought Gaiman from Britain on the strength of Violent Cases and Black Orchid, and their working relationship across Sandman's seven-year run is the clearest single example of what the Vertigo editorial model was for.
Berger recruited Morrison alongside Gaiman and gave Animal Man, Doom Patrol and later The Invisibles the editorial room to be as strange as they were — the experimental end of the imprint's range.

Moore's original proposal used the newly acquired Charlton characters; told that would render them unusable afterwards, he built analogues instead. The result treats the superhero as a political and psychological problem, and asks what a genuinely superhuman being would do to history.

Gibbons held the series to a rigid nine-panel grid and filled it with symmetries, repeated objects and buried rhymes, so that the formal structure carries as much of the argument as the script. The discipline is inseparable from the work's reputation.

Moore wrote the proposal for the Charlton heroes DC had just bought, and the analogues remain traceable: the Question became Rorschach, Blue Beetle became Nite Owl, Captain Atom became Doctor Manhattan, Peacemaker became the Comedian.

Wein edited the series through its early issues, pressing Moore on structure and pacing, and later described the working relationship as a difficult one. He had also edited Moore's Swamp Thing, and it was that run that made the case for handing him an original twelve-issue series in the first place.

Moore understood the Watchmen contract to return the rights once the work went out of print; it never has, so it never did. Disputes over that, over merchandising and over later projects ended his relationship with DC, and he has since declined credit or payment for adaptations of his work.

Watchmen gave DC a permanent commercial and critical asset and a permanent reputational problem: the work most often cited as proof of what comics can do is also the industry's most cited example of how it treats the people who make them.

Wolfman took DC's grown-up sidekicks, added three new characters, and wrote them as an ensemble with continuing relationships and consequences — an approach borrowed frankly from what was working for Marvel's X-Men.

Pérez's detailed figure work and willingness to draw large casts without losing individual expression made the ensemble legible, and his design work on Raven, Cyborg and Starfire gave the book its identity.

Their partnership produced both DC's best-selling title of the early 1980s and the series that demolished its continuity: the commercial standing earned by New Teen Titans is what allowed them to propose Crisis on Infinite Earths.
Leading the Titans gave Grayson an identity independent of Batman, and it was in Wolfman and Pérez's run that he finally broke with him and became Nightwing in 1984.

West was a founding Titan as Kid Flash, and the team's long-form serialised storytelling gave him the accumulated history that made his promotion to the Flash after Crisis feel earned rather than arbitrary.

The 1980 relaunch transformed a periodically cancelled team book into DC's flagship for a decade, and established that sidekicks could be written as adults with their own lives rather than as junior versions of their mentors.

Wolfman proposed the series to solve what editorial regarded as a problem: fifty years of parallel Earths and duplicate characters that made the line unwelcoming. His solution was to destroy the multiverse and merge the survivors into one history.

The commission required Pérez to draw effectively every character DC owned, often dozens to a page, across twelve issues. The double-page spreads of massed heroes became the series' signature and the model for every crossover since.

As DC's editorial leader Giordano authorised a series that would rewrite every title in the line simultaneously, and enforced the coordination across editors that made a line-wide crossover possible for the first time.

Allen died destroying the antimatter cannon, running until he unravelled into the energy that powered his own speed. It was among the first permanent deaths of a major superhero and stood for twenty-three years.

Supergirl was killed saving Superman, and Pérez's image of him carrying her body became the series' defining panel. Post-Crisis editorial then ruled that he must be Krypton's only survivor, keeping her out of continuity for years.

West took the Flash's name in the series' aftermath, the first permanent promotion of a sidekick to his mentor's role at DC and the moment legacy succession became a governing idea rather than an occasional device.

Crisis established the line-wide crossover as a commercial fixture and the periodic continuity reset as company practice. Every subsequent DC relaunch, including the New 52 and Rebirth, is a descendant of the solution it proposed.
Clearing the multiverse created the opening for a total restart of the company's oldest character, and Byrne's miniseries was commissioned to fill it within months of the crossover ending.

Crisis grew directly out of its creators' standing on Titans, and borrowed its method: character-driven serialisation with consequences that stick, applied for the first time to an entire publishing line at once.

Ostrander revived a forgotten 1959 title as a black-ops political thriller: convicted supervillains sent on deniable missions with explosive implants, killed off without warning, and run by a bureaucrat rather than a hero.

Wein co-created Amanda Waller with Ostrander and John Byrne — an uncompromising government administrator with no powers and no interest in being liked, and the most durable original character to come out of DC's late 1980s.

With Kim Yale, Ostrander responded to The Killing Joke by rebuilding the paralysed Barbara Gordon as Oracle, the information broker at the centre of the DC universe — a deliberate refusal to leave the character as someone else's plot device.

McDuffie's work on Justice League and Justice League Unlimited placed Stewart at the centre of the team, giving him a long-running relationship, a military past treated seriously, and the prominence that made him the default Green Lantern for a mass audience.

Johns restored Jordan after a decade in which he had been written as a villain and then killed, attributing the fall to an external parasite. The rehabilitation, and the emotional-spectrum mythology he built afterwards, made Green Lantern one of DC's best-selling franchises for years.

Johns built the crossover around Barry Allen's single selfish act — running back through time to save his mother — and made repairing it require letting her die again, a rare case of an event crossover turning on a personal moral failure.

The altered timeline supplied the in-fiction mechanism for the relaunch: when Barry restored history it came back different, five years younger and with the WildStorm and Vertigo characters folded in alongside the DC ones.

Cancelling and restarting the entire line at once was the most drastic commercial intervention in DC's history. It produced a real short-term sales increase and a lasting loss of the accumulated history that distinguished the company from its competitor.
Lee served as co-publisher for the relaunch and redesigned much of the line's costuming, giving the New 52 a uniform house style built around collars, seams and armour plating that dated quickly.
Snyder's Batman was the relaunch's critical and commercial flagship, and the one New 52 title whose reputation survived the reversal of nearly everything around it.

West was written out of existence by the relaunch, which cut the timeline too short to accommodate a second-generation Flash. His absence became the focus of reader objections to the New 52 as a whole.

Rebirth reversed the relaunch within five years, restoring the marriages, legacies and history it had deleted, and framing the loss in-fiction as a theft to be undone rather than an editorial decision to be defended.

Johns wrote DC Universe: Rebirth #1 as an argument about the company's own values — that continuity, legacy and optimism were assets rather than obstacles — and built it around Wally West trying to get back into a world that has forgotten him.

West's return is the emotional centre of Rebirth, and his restoration was read by readers and by DC alike as a statement that the legacy structure the New 52 had discarded was being reinstated permanently.

Rebirth implicated Doctor Manhattan in the theft of DC's history, setting up Doomsday Clock and folding the Watchmen characters into DC continuity — a commercial decision widely criticised given the circumstances of the original series' creation.

Kahn arrived in 1976 at a company losing badly to Marvel and left in 2002 having introduced royalties and creator incentives, recruited a generation of British writers, backed the direct market, and made DC the industry's prestige publisher.

Levitz spent more than three decades at DC as writer, editor and finally president, helping design the creator-rights reforms of the Kahn years and steering the company through the 1990s speculator crash without the retrenchment that damaged its competitors.

Kahn set the direction and Levitz made the business work, a division of labour that lasted a quarter of a century and covers the period in which nearly all of DC's most celebrated comics were published.

Giordano's decade as editorial leader from 1983 covers Crisis, the Byrne Superman, The Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen, Year One and the mature line that became Vertigo — as concentrated a run of consequential publishing as any editor in the medium has overseen.

Giordano brought O'Neil with him from Charlton to DC in 1968, and the pairing of the editor and the writer runs through the Bronze Age from Green Lantern/Green Arrow to O'Neil's own long tenure editing the Batman line.

Infantino moved from drawing the Silver Age to running the company as editorial director and then publisher, recruiting Kirby and pushing DC towards larger formats and higher prices — an artist's tenure at the top that has no real parallel in the industry.

Lee arrived with the WildStorm acquisition and rose from marquee artist to co-publisher and then to DC's most senior creative posts, shaping the New 52's look and the company's direction for two decades.

Johns wrote or architected most of DC's major events for fifteen years and served as chief creative officer, extending a single writer's editorial preference — that continuity is an asset to be repaired rather than a burden to be cleared — across publishing and screen alike.

Donner's film proved the commercial case for taking DC's characters to the screen at scale, and its eventual decline into camp sequels made Warner receptive to Burton's argument for a darker approach a decade later.

The film's production is also what made the Siegel and Shuster campaign effective: Warner had a costly, heavily publicised release approaching and no appetite for stories about the creators living in poverty.

The resemblance was the substance of National's case: a flying, invulnerable strongman in a caped costume, published in a market where Superman's success had made imitation universal. The suit's outcome shaped what publishers believed they could copy for decades.

DC's own house standards already met most of the new industry code, so the company lost almost nothing while its horror and crime competitors were destroyed. That advantage made DC one of the Code's firmest institutional defenders, and it kept the seal on its covers until 2011.

The industry's defining competition. DC's success with the Justice League prompted Goodman to commission a superhero team book in 1961, and Marvel's rise through the 1960s eventually took the sales lead. The two have exchanged staff continually — Kirby, Ditko, Byrne, Wolfman, Harras and Jim Lee all worked at both — and have co-published crossovers, while remaining each other's principal rival for six decades.

Kirby left in 1970 having received no ownership, no royalties and, in his view, insufficient credit for the characters the company was built on, and having been refused the return of his artwork. The dispute continued for the rest of his life and beyond it, through his heirs' 2009 termination notices and the settlement with Disney in 2014.

It is the central unresolved question in Marvel's history: the company's most valuable assets were produced under an arrangement that gave the man who drew and largely devised them a page rate and nothing else.

Infantino's recruitment of Kirby in 1970 was a direct raid on the competitor then overtaking DC in sales, and was reported as such. The terms he offered — write, draw and edit your own titles, with no editorial supervision — were precisely what Marvel had declined to give.

The League's success is widely credited with prompting Martin Goodman to ask Stan Lee for a superhero team, producing the Fantastic Four in 1961. DC's own commercial triumph is therefore the conventional starting point of the rival line that would displace it within a decade.

Losing the market lead in the early 1970s forced changes at DC that its own success never would have: the recruitment of Marvel's most valuable artist, the editorial overhaul under Jenette Kahn, royalties and creator incentives, and eventually a house style built on prestige rather than volume.

Marvel registered its own Captain Marvel in the late 1960s, so when DC licensed the Fawcett character in 1972 it could not use his name on the cover. The book was published as Shazam! instead, and the wizard's name eventually became the character's — a trademark accident that renamed a hero who had once outsold Superman.

Kirby asked for the title because it was unassigned and selling poorly, so that taking it would not cost anyone work. He used it to seed the Fourth World into existing DC continuity, introducing the DNA Project, a cloned Newsboy Legion and the first appearance of Darkseid before any of his own titles had launched.

Kirby drew the run himself, and DC had his Superman heads redrawn by staff artists to preserve the established house likeness. The correction is visible on the page and remains the clearest illustration of the limits placed on his autonomy even at the company that had recruited him for it.

DC handed Kirby the weakest title on the Superman schedule and got back a book that introduced Apokolips, the Anti-Life Equation and Darkseid. Sales rose sharply on his arrival and the Superman office's discomfort with his handling of the character began almost as quickly.

Kirby wrote the Forever People as young New Genesis emigrants moving through an America of communes, television preachers and hostile police — the Fourth World's argument about free will translated into the idiom of 1971. The book was cancelled after eleven issues with its story unfinished.
The title carries some of Kirby's most experimental DC pages, including photo-collage sequences for the Infinity Man's appearances that no other mainstream comic of the period would have printed.

The Forever People #1 in 1971 carried Darkseid's first full appearance, two months after the Jimmy Olsen cameo. He is introduced not as a monster but as an administrator: unhurried, uninterested in combat, and pursuing a formula rather than a conquest.

Kirby wrote Mister Miracle as the Fourth World's most personal book — an escape artist raised in a prison state, whose every trap is a restatement of the one he grew up in. It ran to eighteen issues, outlasting the other titles, and is the only part of the line to have been revived repeatedly since.

Kirby drew the escapes as engineering problems, filling pages with the machinery of confinement and the mechanisms of getting out of it — the clearest expression at DC of his habit of treating technology as the subject rather than the scenery.

Scott Free appeared in Mister Miracle #1 in 1971, arriving on Earth as an apprentice to an ageing stage escapologist whose name and act he inherits. His Apokolips upbringing is withheld and then revealed across the run, turning the series retrospectively into an escape story about childhood.

Barda arrived in the fourth issue as the commander of Darkseid's Female Furies, sent to retrieve Scott Free and defecting instead. She was written from the start as his equal and his superior in a fight, and the two have been inseparable in every subsequent treatment.

DC cancelled the title in 1974 with the Fourth World story unresolved, then returned to the character repeatedly — in the Justice League's International era, in Grant Morrison's Seven Soldiers, and in Tom King and Mitch Gerads's 2017 series, which won its year's major awards.

Kirby built the character from the Fourth World's central exchange: Highfather's son given to Darkseid under a peace treaty and raised in Granny Goodness's orphanage. Making the victim of that bargain into a professional escape artist is the neatest idea in the whole line.

Kirby created Barda as a soldier bred by Apokolips who walks away from it, and wrote her marriage to Scott Free as settled and equal rather than as a romance to be strung out — an unusual choice for a 1971 superhero comic and the reason the pair have aged better than most of his DC creations.

Orion is Kirby's argument in one figure: Darkseid's son raised by his enemy, whose inherited rage shows whenever his harness fails. The character exists to test whether upbringing can outrun blood, which is the question the entire Fourth World is organised around.

Orion led New Gods from its first issue in 1971, sent from New Genesis to fight the father he was traded away from. Kirby planned the war to end in a confrontation between them; the cancellation left that ending unpublished for years.

Father and son, each raised by the other's enemy under the treaty that exchanged them. Kirby wrote the opposition as inheritance against upbringing rather than good against evil, and prophesied an ending in which one kills the other.

Scott Free is the child Darkseid was given as a hostage and the one person to have escaped Apokolips outright. The pursuit that follows is the Fourth World's demonstration that the Anti-Life Equation has a counter-example walking around.

They meet as prisoner and guard commander on Apokolips, leave together, and are married for most of their publication history. Kirby wrote the partnership as already settled, and later writers have generally treated the marriage as the fixed point the stories happen around.

Scott Free and Barda served through the League's International era in the late 1980s, when the book was played largely for comedy. Placing two Fourth World characters in a sitcom roster is a good measure of how far DC's use of Kirby's material has ranged from his own.

Kirby wrote Kamandi from 1972 as the Fourth World titles were being cancelled around him, and it became his best-selling DC book — a ruined America of animal empires that gave him a new landscape to invent in every issue without the burden of a planned mythology.
Kirby drew the first forty issues, and the series is where his DC-period design work is at its loosest: tiger cavalry, submerged cities, machinery repurposed by species that do not understand it.

The title outlasted the Fourth World that DC had hired Kirby to build, running fifty-nine issues to 1978. That his most commercially successful DC work was the one with no grand structure behind it is a fair summary of how the company and the artist misunderstood each other.

Kirby's four years at DC produced no commercial hit on the scale the company had hoped for, and every one of the Fourth World titles was cancelled mid-story. What they left behind — Darkseid, Apokolips, the New Gods, the Anti-Life Equation — has since become the cosmology the rest of DC's universe is measured against, used by nearly every major event the company has published.

Kirby returned to Marvel in 1975 after the DC titles were cancelled, writing and drawing Captain America and The Eternals there before leaving mainstream comics again. His DC period lasted four years and is the only stretch of his career in which he had full control of his own line.

Morrison has treated the Fourth World as DC's genuine mythology rather than as a set of unused characters, building Seven Soldiers, Final Crisis and much of their Batman work out of Kirby's cosmology and its vocabulary of gods, traps and equations.

Morrison wrote Final Crisis as the war Kirby described, already lost: Darkseid fallen to Earth, the Anti-Life Equation loose and spreading through ordinary people as a formula that ends the capacity to choose. The elliptical, fragmentary structure divided readers as sharply as anything DC published that decade.

The crossover put Darkseid at the centre of DC's continuity for the first time since Kirby created him, treating the Anti-Life Equation not as a weapon to be seized but as an infection already taking hold — the argument for free will the Fourth World was built to make, staged as an apocalypse.

Batman is struck by Darkseid's Omega Sanction and removed from continuity for roughly a year, a death that turned out to be a displacement through time. Handing that beat to a Kirby villain placed the Fourth World at the centre of DC's biggest character franchise.

Nearly forty years after cancellation, the unfinished Fourth World supplied the material for a line-wide crossover: the gods, the war and the equation, brought forward by a writer treating Kirby's cancelled titles as DC's founding scripture rather than as back catalogue.

Goodman set Timely up in 1939 as an extension of his pulp-magazine business, having watched the success of Superman and concluded that comic books were the next profitable format. He registered the company under one of several corporate names he used interchangeably, a habit that would later complicate the legal history of who owned what.

He supplied capital and commercial judgement rather than creative direction, buying the first issue's contents ready-made from an outside packaging shop.

Timely's first publication, cover-dated October 1939, was assembled by Funnies, Inc., an outside studio that supplied complete comics to publishers entering the market. Goodman took the risk on a single issue; when it sold out and a second printing also sold, he committed to a permanent comics line and began hiring his own staff.

Simon and Kirby brought the character to Goodman, who gave it a title of its own rather than a slot in an anthology — an unusual show of confidence for a new creation. Wartime sales approaching a million copies an issue made Timely a significant publisher, and made the terms of Simon and Kirby's profit-sharing arrangement a matter worth arguing over.

The same company under a different name: through the 1950s Goodman's comics carried the globe logo of Atlas News Company, his own distribution arm. The change of branding coincided with a change of content, as the collapse of superhero sales pushed the line into westerns, war, romance, crime, humour and horror.

Continuity of ownership and staff, but not of approach. After the 1957 distribution crisis reduced Atlas to a handful of titles produced almost single-handedly by Stan Lee, the surviving operation began branding its covers as Marvel from 1963, on the back of the superhero line begun with Fantastic Four #1.

The 1954 Code shut down the horror and crime titles that made up a substantial part of Goodman's output, and required every issue to be submitted for approval before distributors would carry it. Combined with the collapse of his own distribution company in 1957, it forced the line down to a fraction of its former size and left Marvel's eventual 1961 relaunch to be attempted with almost no staff.

Superheroes were largely abandoned after the war and revived from 1956, beginning at DC. The two periods differ less in the characters than in the conditions: the Silver Age was made by a smaller, more professionalised industry working under the Comics Code, for a readership that had begun to write in and organise itself.

The transition is usually dated to the early 1970s, marked by Kirby's departure for DC in 1970, the Comics Code revision of 1971, the death of Gwen Stacy in 1973 and the arrival of writers and artists who had grown up as Marvel readers rather than as jobbing professionals in other genres.

Timely was one of the wave of publishers founded in the two years after Superman's 1938 debut, and its wartime peak — Captain America, the Human Torch, the Sub-Mariner — places it among the period's most successful. Like its competitors it collapsed back into other genres once the war ended and superhero sales fell away.

The title is one of the defining artefacts of the period: produced at speed by two creators in their twenties, explicitly propagandistic, hugely popular during the war, and cancelled a few years after it, following the arc of the Golden Age superhero exactly.

Its contents show the form before it settled: an anthology mixing a jungle adventurer and a western gunfighter with two costumed leads, one an artificial man who cannot control his own fire and the other an undersea prince hostile to humanity. Neither would be described as a hero without qualification.

Marvel kept the title in print almost continuously from 1961 until 2015, when it was suspended for three years — a decision many readers attributed to the film rights then sitting with Fox, which Marvel denied. It returned in 2018 as the Fox acquisition proceeded.

Marvel's longest-running and, for most of its history, best-selling title. The company has treated its numbering as a marketing instrument, restarting it from a new first issue several times and then restoring the original count for anniversary numbers.

Rather than cancel the failing title outright in 1970, Marvel kept it in print filled with reprints. That decision is why the 1975 revival could resume the original numbering from issue 94, and why the series Claremont wrote is continuous with the one Lee and Kirby launched.

The title Marvel uses to administer its shared universe: a book whose membership is designed to change, and which the company has repeatedly used to promote characters from elsewhere in the line or to stage the consequences of a crossover.

Marvel cancelled the series after six issues in 1963, kept the character alive in a shared slot in Tales to Astonish, and then renumbered that title to continue the Hulk's original count from issue 102 — an early instance of the company's reluctance to let a numbering run end.

Marvel published the series continuously from 1964 until 1998, sustaining it for fifteen years as a mid-list book before Frank Miller made it a flagship, then relaunched it from a new first issue under the Marvel Knights imprint.

Roy Thomas persuaded Goodman to license Robert E. Howard's character on a small budget, after a more expensive option had been refused. It was Marvel's first significant licensed property and proved that the company could sell comics outside the superhero genre — a lesson applied later to Star Wars, whose licence was credited with keeping Marvel solvent in the late 1970s.

Marvel published seventy issues between 1972 and 1979, and ran a companion black-and-white magazine that fell outside the Comics Code's jurisdiction and could therefore carry material the colour comic could not.

Published as a twelve-issue limited series in 1984-85, a format Marvel had only recently adopted, and coordinated with a Mattel toy line. Its sales made the annual company-wide event a fixture of Marvel's publishing schedule.

A six-issue limited series published in 1991 with tie-ins across the line, at a point when Marvel was publishing crossovers annually and the format had become the main instrument for lifting sales across weaker titles.

Published in 1994 as a four-issue prestige-format series on heavier paper at a higher price — a format Marvel used for work aimed at older readers, and a deliberate contrast to the foil-covered speculator products dominating its schedule that year.

Marvel published the issue with four interlocking covers that assembled into one image, with a fifth gatefold carrying the whole, a device explicitly designed to sell the same comic more than once to the same buyer. The resulting figure was reported as a record and functioned as a warning.

A seven-issue series in 2006-07 with tie-ins running through most of the line, and the clearest demonstration of the model Marvel had settled into: an annual event that every ongoing title is expected to accommodate.

The imprint was created inside Marvel in 2000 as a parallel line, deliberately walled off from the main continuity so that it could restart the characters without disturbing the books that existing readers bought. It ran until 2015, when its universe was folded into the main one during Secret Wars.

An unusual arrangement in which Marvel, short of money and confidence in 1998, contracted an outside studio run by Joe Quesada and Jimmy Palmiotti to produce four of its titles with minimal editorial oversight. The gamble paid off well enough that the imprint's editor was given the whole company two years later.

Epic sat inside Marvel while operating on opposite principles: creators kept ownership of their characters and shared in the profits. Running a creator-owned line alongside a work-for-hire one was Marvel's attempt to answer the rights argument of the early 1980s without changing the terms of its main business.

The imprint's first title and its most successful, launched in 2000 and running for over a decade and a half. Its reception established that a parallel continuity could be sold to new readers without damaging the original line.

The relaunched Daredevil was the imprint's flagship, written by the film director Kevin Smith and drawn by Joe Quesada. Recruiting a name from outside comics to a mid-list superhero title was a deliberate attempt to reach readers who did not visit comic shops, and it worked well enough to become standard practice at Marvel afterwards.

Shooter authorised the imprint in 1982, alongside a royalty scheme and the graphic-novel line, as part of a broader response to the creators' rights pressure that had been building since the 1970s. That the most centralising editor-in-chief in Marvel's history also created its creator-owned line is one of the genuine complications in his record.

Goodwin edited both Epic Illustrated and the comics imprint that grew out of it, and his reputation for handling difficult and idiosyncratic talent without imposing on it was what made the creator-owned arrangement workable in practice.

Creator-owned and specialist titles only became publishable once orders were non-returnable and came from shops whose customers had actively chosen comics. Epic, the graphic-novel line and the direct-market-only series Shooter launched all depended on that arithmetic.

Seven artists could leave the largest publisher in the industry and start a company because the distribution system no longer required a publisher's relationship with newsstand wholesalers. Retailers would order anything their customers would buy, and in 1992 what they would buy was whatever these seven drew.

Non-returnable orders meant publishers took no risk on a large print run, and retailers took all of it. That asymmetry rewarded variant covers, polybagged first issues and relaunches, and allowed print runs to be driven by retailer speculation rather than by readership — until the retailers were left holding the stock.

Burgos wrote and drew the character for Marvel Comics #1 in 1939, taking the idea of an android that ignites in air from science fiction rather than from the Superman template. He decades later attempted to establish a claim to the character and failed, the work having been done for hire.

The Torch led the first issue, presented less as a hero than as a menace: an artificial man created by a scientist, escaping his containment and burning whatever he touches before learning any control.

Everett created the Sub-Mariner for Motion Picture Funnies Weekly, a promotional giveaway published earlier in 1939, and the character was then reprinted and continued in Marvel Comics #1. He took the name from Coleridge and gave the character an explicit resentment of the surface world's incursions into the sea.

Namor's story in the first issue was not new: Everett had drawn it for Motion Picture Funnies Weekly, a giveaway earlier in 1939 that was barely distributed, and most of it was reprinted here with new pages added.

His debut set the tone of the book. Namor arrives hostile to the surface world and stays that way — a protagonist introduced attacking New York, printed alongside an android who burns anything he touches. Timely's first comic established from the outset that its characters would be difficult, which is the quality the company later built a house style on.

Simon conceived the character in 1940 and brought Kirby in to develop him, at a point when American opinion on intervention in Europe was sharply divided. Their decision to put a costumed hero in a fight with Hitler on the first cover was a deliberate political act by two young Jewish creators, and it drew threats to the Timely office as well as sales.

Kirby's contribution was the visual conception and the storytelling: the shield, the propulsive action, and the sheer physical force of the pages, which were unlike anything else on the newsstand in 1940. He returned to the character repeatedly across his career, including a run he wrote and drew himself in the 1970s.

The most successful creative partnership of the Golden Age, working as a self-contained studio that sold complete comics to publishers. Simon handled writing, editing and business, Kirby drove art and storytelling, though both worked across the boundary.

They created Captain America together at Timely, left in 1941 over unpaid profit-sharing, went to National, and after the war invented the romance comic with Young Romance. The partnership dissolved in the mid-1950s after their own publishing venture failed.

The character carried his own title from the start, cover-dated March 1941 and on sale the previous December. Its wartime circulation, reported in the region of a million copies an issue, made him Timely's most valuable property and the company's principal Golden Age success.

Simon packaged the title as well as drawing and writing on it, handling covers, layouts and the business arrangement with Goodman. The studio method he and Kirby used — delivering complete comics rather than pages — gave them unusual leverage for the period.

Kirby pencilled the first ten issues before he and Simon left over unpaid profit-sharing. The pages are notably violent and kinetic by 1941 standards, and established a way of drawing action that the rest of the industry spent the decade catching up with.

The partnership that produced most of what Marvel now sells. Between 1961 and 1970 they made the Fantastic Four, the Hulk, Thor, Iron Man, the X-Men, the Avengers, the Black Panther, the Silver Surfer, Galactus and the Inhumans, working under the Marvel Method: Kirby drew and largely plotted from a loose premise, Lee then dialogued the finished pages.

Because of that process the division of authorship is genuinely difficult to establish, and the two men's accounts diverged sharply and permanently. Kirby left for DC in 1970 feeling under-credited and underpaid; Lee remained the company's public face. The dispute over what each contributed has continued long after both men's deaths.

Lee and Ditko created Spider-Man and Doctor Strange, and produced the first thirty-eight issues of Amazing Spider-Man together. From around the twenty-fifth issue Ditko was plotting the stories himself and receiving a plotting credit, and by the end the two men were reportedly no longer speaking directly and communicated through the office.

Ditko left in 1966 without public explanation and never afterwards discussed the split. He maintained for the rest of his life that he was Spider-Man's co-creator on equal terms, and declined the credit-based payments Marvel later offered.

Lee's account is that, told to produce a superhero team book and considering leaving the industry, he wrote a synopsis for characters who would argue, worry about money and dislike their own powers. The first issue's decision to give them no secret identities and no costumes at all was the clearest signal that the terms had changed.

Kirby designed the four, drew the first hundred issues, and supplied most of what the title became famous for: the Thing's misery, Doctor Doom, the Negative Zone, Galactus, the Inhumans and the Silver Surfer. His account of the origin of the book differs from Lee's, and the disagreement was never resolved.

Fantastic Four #1, cover-dated November 1961, is conventionally taken as the beginning of Marvel as it now exists. Its sales figures and its letters — from readers who wanted more of the arguing and the domestic detail — determined the direction of every title the company launched over the following five years.

Lee scripted the title through its first decade, supplying dialogue over Kirby's completed pages along with the running editorial address to readers — the letters page, the credit boxes and the jokes at the company's own expense — that gave Marvel its public personality.

Kirby drew the title for just over a hundred issues, a stretch containing most of the concepts Marvel still trades on: the Inhumans, the Black Panther, Wakanda, the Negative Zone, Doctor Doom's Latveria and the Silver Surfer.

The Galactus trilogy in issues 48 to 50, produced in 1966, is generally regarded as the peak of his collaboration with Lee — a world-eating entity treated not as a villain to be punched but as an indifferent force of nature, and a herald who defects on aesthetic grounds. The scale of it changed what a superhero comic was assumed to be able to contain.

Lee has said he wanted a teenage hero who was not a sidekick and whose problems continued after the fight ended, and that Goodman objected on the grounds that people dislike spiders and teenagers cannot lead. He put the character in the final issue of a cancelled anthology, where the risk was minimal.

Ditko designed the costume that hides the wearer's age and expression entirely, invented the web-shooters as a mechanical device built by a bright teenager, and drew the character as physically slight and awkward out of costume. The moral shape of the early strip — guilt, obligation, the refusal of easy reward — is largely his.

Eleven pages in a title that was being cancelled, ending with the hero learning that his uncle's killer is the thief he had chosen not to stop. The issue turned out to be one of Marvel's best-selling of the year, though the figures did not arrive until months after publication.

Ditko drew all eleven pages and designed the costume, the web-shooters and the character's physical awkwardness out of it. He drew the origin as a small domestic tragedy rather than an adventure: the decisive moment is a teenager declining to intervene, and the consequence arrives in a caption at the end.

Lee scripted the story and wrote the closing caption on power and responsibility that has followed the character ever since. He placed it in a title that was being cancelled, where a failure would cost the company nothing.

The sales returns for the cancelled anthology's last issue were strong enough that Goodman, who had objected to the character, authorised an ongoing series. Amazing Spider-Man #1 followed in March 1963 and the character became Marvel's best-selling property within a few years.

Ditko drew the first thirty-eight issues and plotted the later ones alone, creating Doctor Octopus, the Green Goblin, the Sandman and most of the character's enduring antagonists. His departure in 1966, at the height of the title's success, was abrupt and never publicly explained.

Lee scripted the title for roughly its first hundred issues, across the Ditko and Romita eras, and used it more than any other book to develop Marvel's characteristic mixture of melodrama, self-deprecation and continuing personal difficulty.

Romita took over from Ditko in 1966 and the title reached its highest sales under him. Coming from romance comics, he made the cast more conventionally attractive and expanded the relationship material, introducing Mary Jane Watson and taking the strip further towards serialised soap opera.

Lee has described the Hulk as an attempt to combine Frankenstein's monster with Jekyll and Hyde — making the audience sympathise with the creature — using the monster formula Marvel had been publishing throughout the 1950s but attaching it to a hero.

Kirby designed and drew the character for the first issues in 1962, giving him a heavy, brutish silhouette closer to Marvel's recent monster comics than to a superhero. The Hulk was printed grey in the first issue and changed to green from the second because the grey reproduced inconsistently.

The original series was cancelled after six issues, an early failure for the new line, and the character survived only because Marvel kept using him elsewhere — as a founding and immediately departing Avenger, and then in a shared slot in Tales to Astonish — before he regained a title of his own.

Lee has said he reasoned that the only way to top a very strong hero was a god, and turned to Norse myth as material in the public domain. The first script was written by his brother Larry Lieber from Lee's outline.

Kirby's long-standing interest in mythology took the strip well beyond its superhero premise, and the Asgard material he designed and largely plotted through the 1960s — the Rainbow Bridge, the Destroyer, the origin sequences of the gods — is among the most visually ambitious work in American comics of the period.

Lee later said he had set himself the problem of making readers care about a wealthy arms manufacturer profiting from a war they opposed. The character's dependence on the device keeping him alive gave him a permanent vulnerability, and the first script was written by Larry Lieber with art by Don Heck over Kirby's design.

Kirby designed the original armour and drew the character's earliest cover appearances; Don Heck drew the debut story itself. The bulky grey suit, replaced within an issue by gold and then red and gold, reflected Kirby's habitual interest in industrial machinery worn as a body.

Lee has said the mutant premise came partly from the difficulty of inventing a fresh accident for every new character: being born with powers explained a whole population at once. He also gave the team the least successful launch of the 1963 books, and the title was cancelled into reprints seven years later.

Kirby designed the original five students, Professor X and Magneto, and drew the first seventeen issues. The essential opposition he set up — a teacher urging patience with a hostile public against a survivor who has concluded that patience is naive — has outlasted every other element of the concept.

The team's 1963 title sold poorly enough to be reduced to reprints in 1970. Its 1975 revival with an entirely new cast, and the run that followed, turned the same numbered series into the best-selling comic in America — an unusually complete reversal for a book that had already been given up on.

Lee assembled the team from characters who already had their own titles, a solution to a schedule problem that also demonstrated to readers that Marvel's books occupied a single world. He established the rotating membership almost immediately, in the second issue.
Kirby drew the first eight issues and designed the team's original line-up and its earliest antagonists. His decision in issue 4 to revive Captain America gave the new Marvel universe a usable past.

The team was assembled in September 1963 from characters who already had their own books, partly as a way of filling a schedule gap. Its fourth issue revived Captain America from suspended animation, folding Timely's Golden Age into the new continuity and giving the modern Marvel universe a past.

Lee dialogued the character's 1966 debut and, with Kirby, made the decision to introduce a Black hero as a head of state and a scientist who outmanoeuvres the Fantastic Four on first meeting rather than as a sidekick or a supporting figure.

The choice was deliberate and, for a mainstream American comic published in the year of the Voting Rights Act's first full application, unusual: T'Challa's Wakanda was not a colonised territory awaiting rescue but a technologically advanced nation that had never been conquered. Lee later gave the character a brief spell as a member of the Avengers to keep him in print.

Kirby designed the character and Wakanda, an African nation never colonised and technologically ahead of the rest of the world — an inversion of how the continent was routinely drawn in American popular culture at the time. Preliminary art shows an earlier version named the Coal Tiger.

T'Challa appeared in Fantastic Four #52, cover-dated July 1966, as the first Black superhero in mainstream American comics — some months before the political party of the same name was founded. Marvel briefly renamed him the Black Leopard in the 1970s to avoid the association, before reverting.

Kirby added the Surfer to the Galactus story without discussing it beforehand, on the reasoning that a being of that scale would send someone ahead of him. Lee, seeing the pages, took the character in an unexpected direction as a philosophical exile, and the two men afterwards gave different accounts of who had made him what he became.

The Surfer and Galactus appeared in Fantastic Four #48 to #50 in 1966, a sequence widely regarded as the high point of the Lee and Kirby collaboration and the moment Marvel's scale expanded from New York to the cosmos.

Ditko originated the strip almost entirely, and its importance was visual: the other dimensions were drawn as abstract, folding geometries with no precedent in commercial American comics. The work found an audience on college campuses in the mid-1960s well beyond Marvel's usual readership.

Lee named the character and wrote the dialogue, and credited Ditko with proposing the concept — a magician hero — in the first place. He gave the strip its incantatory vocabulary, which readers quoted back at the company for years.

Lee devised a hero whose disability is the source of his abilities, and gave him a day job as a defence lawyer, extending the pattern of ordinary professional difficulty he had established with Spider-Man.

Everett, one of Timely's founding artists, returned to co-create the character in 1964, drawing the first issue over Kirby's design for the costume and billy club. The link made Daredevil a direct connection between Marvel's 1939 generation and its 1960s one.

The character carried his own title from April 1964, one of the last of the Lee-era launches. It sold modestly for fifteen years, which is largely why Marvel was willing to let Frank Miller do something unusual with it.

The method was in part a solution to Lee's workload: editing and scripting a dozen titles at once made full scripts impossible, so he supplied outlines or conversations and dialogued the finished pages. It let a very small staff produce a full line, and it gave Marvel's books their distinctive voice, since the words were written to art that already existed.

Kirby's side of the method was the greater part of the storytelling: given a premise, he decided what happened, how many pages it took, what the settings and machinery looked like, and frequently added characters nobody had asked for. He often pencilled margin notes to guide the dialogue that would be added over his work.

The working process and the period are inseparable: the density of invention in Marvel's 1961-1966 output is a direct consequence of artists plotting visually at speed, and so is the permanent ambiguity about who created what, which no later account has been able to resolve.
The November 1961 issue is the conventional starting point for Marvel's part in the Silver Age, and the title remained the line's engine of invention for the following five years.

The issue is the period's clearest demonstration of how Marvel's method differed: a hero introduced in a cancelled anthology, defined by guilt and failure, whose commercial success was discovered only afterwards from the sales returns.

Lee's contribution to the period was as much editorial and rhetorical as authorial: he set the tone of the dialogue, invented the direct address to readers, and organised a line of titles that behaved as one continuous world.

Kirby supplied the period's visual vocabulary and a large proportion of its concepts, drawing and largely plotting the majority of Marvel's significant titles between 1961 and 1970 at a rate no other artist matched.

Working under the Marvel Method, he received a premise of a sentence or two and returned finished pages carrying the plot, the pacing and usually the new characters as well; Lee then dialogued them. The arrangement is why the period's output is so dense with invention, and why the question of who created what has never been settled to anyone's satisfaction.

Ditko's two strips gave the period its other register: the cramped, anxious realism of Spider-Man's New York and the abstract dimensional geometry of Doctor Strange, neither of which resembled anything else being published.

Goodman remained publisher through the 1960s expansion and sold the company to Perfect Film & Chemical in 1968, staying on for several years afterwards. His distribution deal with a rival that was also DC's distributor had capped Marvel's output at eight titles a month in the early 1960s, a constraint that shaped which characters shared books.

Lee was editor from 1941 and editor-in-chief through the whole of the Silver Age until 1972, when he became publisher. Beyond the writing, he built the company's public voice — the credit boxes, the Bullpen Bulletins, the running address to the reader — which turned a publishing line into something readers felt they belonged to.

Lee moved up to publisher in 1972 and handed editorial control to Thomas, who had been his effective deputy. The change marked a generational shift: Thomas was the first editor-in-chief who had come to the job as a comics fan rather than as a jobbing magazine professional.

Thomas resigned the post in 1974, unwilling to give up writing for administration, and Wein took it on. The following four years saw the job change hands four times, as each holder found the workload incompatible with the writing careers they had no wish to abandon.

Wein held the post for about a year before returning to writing, and Wolfman took over in 1975. The rapid turnover reflected a job that combined administering an expanding line with the writing careers none of its holders wanted to give up.

Wolfman left the post in 1976 and Conway, then in his mid-twenties and already writing Amazing Spider-Man, took it on for a matter of months before stepping back to write full time. His was the fourth change of editor-in-chief in three years, and the turnover is the clearest measure of how unworkable the job had become: an expanding line to administer, and no holder willing to give up the writing that had got them the offer.

Conway's tenure was short, and Goodwin — older, more experienced as an editor, and widely trusted by creators — took over in 1976 and steadied the position before handing it to his associate editor two years later.

Goodwin left in 1978 and Shooter, his associate editor, took over. The contrast in method was total: Goodwin had governed by persuasion and goodwill, Shooter by schedules, standards and central authority — which was, by most accounts, what the company then needed and what made him unpopular.

Shooter was removed in 1987 after accumulated conflict with staff and star creators, several of whom had left for DC or independent publishers. DeFalco was appointed with an explicit brief to decentralise, giving individual editors and popular artists far more autonomy.

DeFalco left in 1994 and Marvel spent roughly a year with no single editor-in-chief, running five semi-independent editorial groups competing with each other. The experiment was abandoned and Harras, who had run the most successful of the groups, was given the whole line in 1995.

Harras left in 2000 after five years spanning bankruptcy, collapsing sales and Heroes Reborn. Quesada, who had come in from outside as an artist running a contracted imprint, replaced him — the first artist and the first outsider to hold the job.
Quesada moved up to chief creative officer in 2011 after eleven years, and Alonso, who had edited several of the line's most successful books, replaced him.

Alonso left in 2017 and Cebulski, previously the company's international talent scout, took over — the first editor-in-chief whose background was primarily in recruiting creators rather than in editing or making comics.
Thomas ran editorial from 1972 to 1974, presiding over the expansion into horror, sword-and-sorcery and licensed properties that the relaxed Comics Code and his own interests made possible.
Goodwin held the post from 1976 to 1978 and is generally credited with stabilising a job that had changed hands four times in as many years, governing by persuasion rather than by imposed standards.

Shooter's nine years brought the line onto schedule, introduced royalties and returned original artwork to some creators, while centralising editorial judgement to a degree that many writers and artists found intolerable. Both the discipline and the resentment are usually cited as reasons for what followed: a decade of strong sales, and a steady loss of star talent.

DeFalco ran the company from 1987 to 1994 through its highest-selling years, having deliberately devolved authority to individual editors and star artists — a policy that produced enormous sales and left Marvel exposed when those artists departed.

Harras held the post from 1995 to 2000, covering bankruptcy, collapsing sales, the loss of talent to Image, and the Heroes Reborn experiment that outsourced the Avengers and Fantastic Four to former Marvel artists.

Quesada's eleven years reoriented Marvel around writers rather than artists, brought in talent from film, television and independent comics, ended participation in the Comics Code, and pushed the line towards collected editions sold in bookshops. Marvel's recovery from near-irrelevance in publishing terms dates from this period.

Alonso's six years widened who appeared in and made Marvel comics, and relied heavily on frequent line-wide relaunches to keep first issues on the shelves — a tactic that lifted individual orders while making the line harder to follow.
Cebulski has run editorial since 2017, in a period when the publishing line operates alongside a far larger film and television business built on the same characters.

As executive editor Gruenwald was the arbiter of continuity across the whole line for most of the 1980s and 1990s, and the driving force behind the Official Handbook of the Marvel Universe, which catalogued every character the company had published. His care for internal consistency shaped how Marvel's shared world was administered.

Harras ran the X-Men group through its commercial peak, when the line accounted for a large proportion of Marvel's sales. His preference for artist-driven storytelling contributed to Chris Claremont's departure in 1991, and to the friction that preceded the Image walkout the following year.

Quesada drew the Marvel Knights relaunch, written by the film director Kevin Smith, in a moody, high-contrast style that set the imprint's visual identity and made the case for his own editorial judgement.

Quesada and Jimmy Palmiotti pitched their studio to a company that had just emerged from bankruptcy and had little to lose on four underperforming titles. The imprint's success made the case that Marvel's problem was editorial rather than commercial, and put its editor in charge of the company.

Jemas cut the number of titles sharply, ended the practice of accepting returns, and pushed for stories a new reader could pick up cold. His interventions in editorial matters and his public combativeness made him widely disliked among creators, but the commercial restructuring he carried out with Quesada was substantially effective.

Jemas argued that four decades of accumulated continuity had made Marvel's titles impenetrable to anyone new, and pushed for a parallel line starting the characters over in the present day. Quesada was initially sceptical; the commercial result settled the argument.

Under Jemas and Quesada, Marvel withdrew from the Comics Code in 2001 and introduced its own age-rating system. The Code had governed the content of American comics since 1954, and Marvel's departure — as the largest publisher — effectively ended its remaining authority.

In 1971 the US Department of Health, Education and Welfare asked Marvel to address drug abuse in a comic. The resulting three-issue Spider-Man story was refused the Code's seal because it depicted drugs at all, and Stan Lee published it without approval.

The issues sold well and drew favourable coverage, and the Code was revised later that year to permit drug storylines presented negatively, along with vampires, werewolves and other classic monsters. It was the first public demonstration that the Code could be defied without commercial penalty.

The 1971 revision lifted the ban on vampires and other gothic monsters that had stood since 1954, and Marvel moved into horror immediately. The Tomb of Dracula, Werewolf by Night and Ghost Rider all follow directly from that change in the rules.

The title exemplifies the period's move outside the superhero genre: a licensed pulp property, published in colour and in a magazine format outside the Comics Code, which sustained Marvel commercially through the 1970s.
The series belongs to the horror revival that the 1971 Code revision made possible, and to the period's willingness to sustain a title with a stable creative team and a continuing cast over years.

The revival's internationalism, and its interest in characters defined by where they came from and what they had survived, are characteristic of a period in which Marvel's writers had grown up reading the company's own earlier work.

The character belongs squarely to the period's turn towards contemporary urban settings and the influence of current cinema, and to Marvel's cautious first attempts at putting Black protagonists at the centre of its titles rather than in supporting roles.

Claremont belongs to the generation of writers who arrived as readers, and his method — long-running subplots, characters who change over years — depends on the assumption of a committed audience that the direct market was beginning to supply.

Thomas acquired the licence cheaply and wrote the series for its first decade, adapting Howard's stories and inventing new ones in the same idiom. Early sales were poor enough that cancellation was discussed; the title survived to run for over two hundred issues and to establish licensed adaptation as a reliable part of Marvel's business.

Buscema took over the art from 1973 and drew Conan on and off for two decades, in a heavy, muscular style that became the standard visual language of sword-and-sorcery comics and influenced the character's depiction well outside Marvel.
