Thomas wrote the Avengers for most of the late 1960s and early 1970s, including the Kree-Skrull War, a nine-issue interstellar storyline that was among the first extended serialised epics in Marvel's superhero line and a direct ancestor of the crossover event.

Adams drew part of the Kree-Skrull War in 1971-72, bringing his photographic anatomy and unconventional page layouts to a nine-issue interstellar storyline that was among Marvel's first extended serialised epics.

Adams drew nine issues in 1969 and 1970 — the run from issue 56 to 63, and issue 65, at the end of the original run and shortly before cancellation. The work is remembered for its anatomy and layouts rather than its sales, and it is often cited as evidence that the title's early failure was not for want of talent.

Wolfman wrote nearly the entire seventy-issue run, treating Dracula as an arrogant aristocrat with genuine grievances rather than as a monster, and holding a continuing cast of hunters together across seven years of serial storytelling — an unusual degree of stability for a 1970s title.
Colan drew every issue, an unbroken seven-year run rare in the period, and his tonal, shadow-built pages gave the series a visual character no other Code-approved horror comic achieved.

Conway took over the title at twenty and wrote The Night Gwen Stacy Died in 1973, in which the hero's attempt to save his girlfriend from a fall kills her instead. Superhero comics had generally treated such losses as reversible; this one was not, and it is widely treated as the point at which the Silver Age's assumptions ended.

Gerber created Howard the Duck for Marvel as work for hire, watched it become a commercial success including a newspaper strip, was removed from the character, and sued in 1980 to establish ownership. The case was settled out of court; he did not regain the character, but the suit — and the Destroyer Duck comic he and Kirby produced to fund it — made creators' rights a public argument rather than a private grievance.

Gerber's 1980 suit over Howard the Duck was one of the first attempts by a Marvel creator to establish ownership of a character made under work-for-hire terms, and the fundraising comic he made with Kirby turned it into a public campaign.

Kirby's campaign to recover his original artwork from Marvel ran through the 1980s and became the defining case of the issue. Marvel initially offered to return a few dozen pages of the thousands it held, and only on condition that he sign away any claim; a public campaign by other creators eventually secured a larger return.

His heirs served copyright termination notices in 2009, arguing the 1960s work had not been made for hire. Marvel and Disney litigated, and the case was settled in 2014 shortly before the Supreme Court was to consider it. Marvel has since credited him on its films.

Simon pursued a claim to Captain America's copyright across four decades, filing in the 1960s and again in the 1990s under the renewal provisions of copyright law. He reached a settlement with Marvel in 2003 that acknowledged his creation of the character.

Adams used his commercial standing to press publishers on behalf of other creators, organising support for the return of original artwork to Kirby and campaigning successfully for DC to acknowledge and pay Superman's creators. He was among the few figures of his generation willing to spend his own leverage on the issue.

Marvel's position throughout has been that work commissioned and paid for at a page rate belongs to the company. Every major concession — royalties, the return of artwork, the Epic imprint, screen credits for Kirby — came after external pressure rather than before it.

Kirby left in 1970 for DC, where he was given editorial control over his own titles for the first time and produced the Fourth World books — New Gods, Mister Miracle and The Forever People — a connected mythology conceived and written as well as drawn by him. The move ended the collaboration that had made Marvel and left the company drawing on his inventions for decades afterwards.

Ditko left Marvel in 1966 at the height of Spider-Man's success and worked afterwards at Charlton, DC and in self-published work. He never gave an account of why, declined interviews for the rest of his life, and continued to insist on his co-authorship of the character without seeking to profit from the claim.

Wein wrote the character into The Incredible Hulk in 1974 as a short-tempered Canadian agent sent to deal with the Hulk, intended as a one-off antagonist with a national identity Marvel had not used before. Nothing in the appearance suggested he would become the company's most popular character.

As art director Romita designed the costume and the claws, which he drew as part of the gloves rather than as part of the man — an ambiguity later writers resolved in a much more disturbing direction. Herb Trimpe drew the character's first published appearance from that design.

A cameo in issue 180 and a full appearance in 181, cover-dated late 1974. The issues are now among the most valuable comics of the decade, which was not remotely foreseeable at the time: the character was a guest antagonist in someone else's book.

Wein and Dave Cockrum were asked to revive a title that had been running reprints for five years, and chose to replace the cast entirely with an international team, partly with overseas licensing in mind. The decision gave the book something the original had lacked: characters with genuinely different histories and reasons for being there.

Storm was created by Wein and Dave Cockrum for the 1975 revival: an American-born woman raised in Cairo and Kenya, worshipped as a goddess before joining the team. Cockrum's design and the character's self-possession made her stand out immediately from a cast of new arrivals.

Storm appeared in the 1975 revival as one of the replacement team, introduced in Kenya where she has been venerated as a rain goddess and recruited by Professor X — an origin unlike any other member's, and one Claremont returned to for years afterwards.

Claremont wrote her over sixteen years from a reserved newcomer into the team's field leader, including a long stretch in which she had lost her powers entirely and commanded on judgement alone — an unusual arc to give a character in a genre organised around abilities.

Wolverine joined in the 1975 revival almost by accident, having been available and Canadian when Wein wanted an international team. Within a decade he was the title's most popular character and the strongest single argument for the new line-up's success.

The one-shot's reception led Marvel to resume the numbered series with the new cast from issue 94, with Chris Claremont writing and Dave Cockrum and then John Byrne drawing.

What had been a cancelled title filled with reprints became, within six years, the best-selling comic in America and the centre of a family of spin-off books that carried the company through the 1980s. The revival also set the pattern Marvel returned to repeatedly afterwards: keep the numbering, replace the cast, and let a long-form writer build on the accumulated history.

Claremont wrote the title continuously from 1975 to 1991, developing subplots over years, aging his cast, and turning the mutant premise into a sustained argument about prejudice, assimilation and separatism.

He created or co-created Rogue, Kitty Pryde, Mystique, Gambit and Sabretooth, and wrote a range of prominent women characters unusual for mainstream comics of the period. His departure in 1991, after losing control of the direction to the artists then driving sales, ended the run and the era.

Byrne drew the title from 1977 to 1981 and co-plotted with Claremont, a collaboration that produced The Dark Phoenix Saga and Days of Future Past. The two argued frequently over direction — Byrne wanted Wolverine and Cyclops handled differently — and the friction is generally credited with sharpening the work.

More than any other writer, Claremont determined what the X-Men are: a found family with long memories, internal politics and a metaphorical reach that later writers and film-makers have all worked within. Almost every X-Men adaptation draws primarily on his sixteen years.

The story took a founding member of the team, gave her limitless power, and had her destroy an inhabited star system before choosing to die. Claremont and Byrne had planned a lesser punishment; Jim Shooter insisted that a character responsible for billions of deaths could not simply return to the team, and the ending was rewritten.
Byrne drew and co-plotted the storyline, and argued against the ending: he and Claremont had intended Jean Grey to survive, and both objected when Jim Shooter insisted the consequences be permanent.

Issues 129 to 138, published in 1980, and the point at which the title's reputation was made. It demonstrated that a monthly superhero comic could carry a tragedy through to an irreversible end, and it has been adapted more often than any other X-Men story.

Byrne wrote and drew the title from 1981 to 1986, a run generally regarded as the best treatment of the characters since Kirby's. He restored the family dynamic, gave Sue Storm a substantially expanded role, and worked in a visual idiom that acknowledged Kirby's storytelling without imitating his drawing.

Miller became writer as well as artist in 1981 and rebuilt the series as crime fiction: the Kingpin promoted from a Spider-Man villain into the character's permanent antagonist, the assassin Elektra introduced and killed, and Hell's Kitchen made a real place with its own economy of violence. His 1986 story Born Again, drawn by David Mazzucchelli, dismantled the hero's life entirely.

Miller joined as artist in 1979 before taking over the writing, and his layouts — heavy black areas, sudden silence, panels borrowed from film and from Japanese comics — changed the book's character before a word of his script appeared.

Every subsequent version of the character — in comics, television and film — proceeds from Miller's: the Catholic guilt, the criminal geography of the neighbourhood, and the sense that this is a man whose choices routinely make his own life worse.

Shooter wrote the twelve-issue series himself, developed in coordination with a Mattel toy line that needed a story to support it. Its commercial success established the line-wide crossover as a repeatable device, and mainstream superhero publishing has been organised around annual events ever since.
The Avengers were the largest contingent on the constructed battle planet, and the storyline's consequences ran back through their title for years afterwards.
The X-Men were placed on the battle planet as a separate faction refusing to take orders from the Avengers, reflecting their commercial independence from the rest of the line at the time.

Gruenwald wrote the character for a decade from 1985, and his central storyline had the hero stripped of the identity by a government commission and replaced by a more compliant successor — a direct test of whether the character belongs to the state or to the ideals it claims. It set the pattern for how later writers use him.

Starlin created Thanos in 1973 while a young artist working on Iron Man, and has said the character emerged from a psychology course and from an interest in death as a subject. He wrote him as a figure who courts annihilation as a lover, which distinguishes him from the conquest-driven villains around him.

Starlin returned to his character in 1991 for a six-issue crossover, drawn by George Perez and then Ron Lim, in which Thanos assembles absolute power and erases half of all living things. It combined his metaphysical preoccupations with the event format Marvel had by then made routine.

The story is built entirely around him: Thanos acquires the six gems, kills half of all living things to impress Death, and is defeated less by the assembled heroes than by his own conviction that he does not deserve what he has taken.

Busiek retold Marvel's first three decades from the point of view of a news photographer who never enters the heroes' world, and who becomes steadily less certain that their arrival was good for anyone. Published at the height of the speculator market, it argued that this material was worth taking seriously as history.

Ross painted the series in gouache from photographic reference, giving costumed figures the weight and light of real bodies. Set against the stylisation dominant in 1994, the approach made familiar characters look strange and monumental, which was the point of the book.

McFarlane's run from 1988 made him one of the first artists whose name alone moved the title's sales, with a style built on contorted poses and dense, irregular webbing. He also redesigned the alien symbiote costume into the look that became Venom.
Lee's work on the established title from 1989 made him the line's most sought-after artist within two years, and his redesigns of several characters' costumes remained standard for a decade.

Lee drew and co-plotted the launch of a second X-Men title, published with four interlocking covers and a fifth gatefold edition. Around eight million copies were sold, still the record for a single comic-book issue — a figure that reflected retailers and speculators buying multiples rather than eight million readers.

Claremont scripted the record-breaking issue and left the title within months, having lost control of the direction to the artist whose name was selling it. The best-selling comic ever published was also the end of the run that had made the franchise.

The issue is the boom's defining artefact: five variant covers designed to be bought as a set, an enormous print run set by retailer orders rather than by readership, and a sales figure of roughly eight million that was reported as a triumph while describing a market buying the same comic five times over.

It remains the best-selling single comic book on record, and the record is itself the clearest measure of how far orders had detached from readers — the number was never approached again once speculative buying stopped.

Liefeld created the character with Fabian Nicieza in New Mutants #98 in 1991 as a costumed mercenary in the mould of the period's antiheroes. The comedic, fourth-wall-breaking version that made him popular was developed by later writers, particularly Joe Kelly, several years afterwards.

McFarlane was the central organiser of the 1992 walkout, having concluded that the artists generating Marvel's sales had no share in what they created and no prospect of getting one. Spawn, his creator-owned title, went on to sell in numbers comparable to Marvel's best.

Lee left immediately after drawing the best-selling comic book ever published, which made the argument for the founders better than anything they could say: the sales belonged to the artists' names, and the characters belonged to Marvel.

At Image he ran WildStorm, one of the studios the founders operated independently under the shared imprint, and the arrangement he left for — full ownership of what he created — was the specific thing Marvel had refused. He sold WildStorm to DC in a deal agreed in 1998 and effective from January 1999, and eventually became that company's publisher.
Liefeld was among the youngest and most commercially conspicuous of the founders, having demonstrated with X-Force that an artist's name could sell several million copies of a comic nobody had read.

The 1992 departure removed several of Marvel's highest-selling artists at once and set up a competitor whose entire pitch was that creators keep what they make. Image took a substantial share of the market within a year, and forced the ownership question into the open at exactly the moment Marvel's own finances were about to fail.

Marvel expanded on the assumption that the boom would hold, buying trading-card companies and a distributor and taking on debt against future sales. When the speculative demand disappeared, the revenue supporting that structure went with it, and the company filed for Chapter 11 protection in December 1996.

Perelman's MacAndrews & Forbes bought Marvel in 1989 and took it public in 1991, then used the company to acquire Fleer, SkyBox, the Heroes World distributor and a stake in Toy Biz, financed with debt.

The attempt to distribute Marvel's own comics through Heroes World damaged relationships with retailers and drove the rest of the industry into an exclusive arrangement with a single rival distributor, contracting the whole market. When sales fell, the debt could not be serviced.

The debt raised against Marvel during Perelman's ownership, the acquisitions made on the assumption of continued growth — Fleer, SkyBox, a stake in Toy Biz — and the decision to buy the Heroes World distributor and supply retailers directly together left the company unable to meet its obligations when sales fell.

The distribution move was the most damaging: it collapsed Marvel's own supply chain, pushed the rest of the industry to an exclusive deal with Diamond, and cost sales at exactly the moment the speculative market disappeared. Marvel filed for Chapter 11 in December 1996, and Perelman lost control of the company in the fight with bondholders that followed.

The bankruptcy was resolved in 1998 not by Marvel's owners but by its toy licensee: Toy Biz merged with the publisher to form Marvel Enterprises, after a two-year court fight between Perelman and bondholders led by Carl Icahn. The company that made the action figures ended up owning the characters.
Perlmutter controlled the toy company that held Marvel's action-figure licence, and used it as the vehicle to acquire the publisher out of bankruptcy in 1998.
Arad ran Toy Biz's creative side, designing toys from Marvel characters, and drew from that the argument he later pressed on the whole company: that the films were what would sell everything else.

The 1998 merger left Perlmutter and Arad running Marvel, and shifted the company's centre of gravity decisively away from publishing. From that point the comics were increasingly valued as a source of characters for toys, licensing and film rather than as the business itself.

Perlmutter's tight control of costs restored profitability in the early 2000s, and his willingness to borrow against the film rights to a group of characters financed Marvel Studios' first self-produced films — the decision on which everything that followed depended.

Bendis retold an origin that had originally taken eleven pages across six issues, in a dialogue-heavy style borrowed from his crime comics. The pacing was designed for collected editions rather than for monthly readers, and its success set the storytelling template for Marvel's next decade.

Bendis dissolved the team in 2004 and rebuilt it around Spider-Man, Wolverine and Luke Cage, moving the title from a legacy book to the centre of the line. The structure he established — the Avengers as the venue for the line's biggest characters and its annual crossovers — is the one the films inherited.

Bendis and Sara Pichelli introduced Miles in 2011, after the Ultimate line's Peter Parker was killed, and Bendis has cited the visibility of a Black president and his own adopted daughter as part of the reasoning. The character drew mainstream press coverage and some hostility, and was eventually established alongside Peter Parker in the main continuity.

Miles was created for the Ultimate line, where the death of that continuity's Peter Parker had left the identity vacant — an outcome only possible in a continuity that was allowed to make permanent changes.

Miles took the identity in the Ultimate line after that continuity's Peter Parker died, rather than replacing him in the main one. The arrangement — two Spider-Men coexisting, the newer one from a different background — proved durable, and Into the Spider-Verse made it the version most widely known outside comics.

Millar split the entire line over a law requiring superhumans to register with the government, setting Iron Man's compliance against Captain America's refusal, and wrote it explicitly against the background of post-2001 arguments about security and liberty. It was among Marvel's best-selling storylines of the decade and ended with Captain America's assassination.

Millar's The Ultimates recast the Avengers as a government weapons programme with a public-relations problem, in a style pitched somewhere between superhero comic and political thriller. Several of its choices, including a Nick Fury drawn to resemble Samuel L. Jackson, were carried over into Marvel's films.
Tony Stark leads the pro-registration side, arguing that superhumans are unaccountable and must be licensed. The story left the character widely disliked by readers for several years afterwards.

Captain America leads the resistance to registration and is assassinated on the courthouse steps at the story's end — the clearest use yet of the character to set a national ideal against the state that claims it.

Brubaker rebuilt the title as a Cold War espionage story and brought back Bucky Barnes, whose 1940s death had been one of the few in superhero comics treated as permanent, as a brainwashed assassin. The Winter Soldier was created for the comics in 2005 and became the basis of one of the most admired Marvel films.

Hickman wrote the title from 2009 as a story about scientific ambition and family across generations, building a long structure that eventually fed into his Avengers work and the 2015 Secret Wars, which destroyed and rebuilt the Marvel universe.

Hickman wrote Avengers and New Avengers together from 2012, one expanding the team to dozens of members and the other reducing it to a handful of people secretly destroying inhabited worlds to save their own. The two strands converged in the 2015 Secret Wars.

House of X and Powers of X in 2019 reset the franchise entirely, relocating mutants to a sovereign island nation with its own laws, economy and diplomacy. It replaced the decades-old premise of a persecuted minority seeking acceptance with something closer to a state pursuing its own interests, and reorganised the whole line around it.

Coates wrote the title from 2016, opening with a popular insurgency that questions whether a hereditary monarch has any right to rule, and treating Wakanda as a state with a political history rather than a backdrop. He came to it as a reader and essayist rather than a comics professional, and the run drew an audience largely from outside the direct market.

Goodwin developed the character with John Romita Sr. and George Tuska in 1972: a man wrongly imprisoned who gains unbreakable skin in a prison experiment and sets up in business as a hero for hire. He was the first Black superhero to headline his own ongoing American comic.

Romita designed the character in 1972, working from the blaxploitation films then in cinemas; George Tuska drew the series itself. The costume — chain belt, open shirt, steel headband — dates the character precisely to its moment.

Wilson developed the character with editor Sana Amanat and artist Adrian Alphona in 2014: a Pakistani-American Muslim teenager in Jersey City whose faith and family are ordinary texture rather than the subject of the book. It became one of Marvel's strongest sellers in collected editions and reached a readership largely outside comic shops.

Claremont wrote Storm for sixteen years, through her arrival, her assumption of leadership, the loss of her powers and a long stretch commanding the team without them. The arc is among the most sustained pieces of character writing in mainstream superhero comics.

X-Force #1 in 1991, polybagged with one of five trading cards to encourage multiple purchases, sold several million copies. It is a clean example of the period's method: the sales came from the packaging and the artist's name rather than from readers wanting the story inside.
McFarlane's 1990 Spider-Man #1, which he wrote and drew, was issued in multiple cover variants and sold in the millions. It established the template the rest of the boom followed.

Arad pushed the licensing deals that put Marvel's characters into other studios' films, arguing that a successful film sold every other product the company made. The fee Marvel received was small relative to the film's take, a disparity that shaped the later decision to produce in-house.

Arad was an executive producer on the film that finally brought Marvel's most valuable character to the screen, after most of a decade in which competing claims to the rights left the property tied up in litigation while the company itself went into bankruptcy.

It vindicated the argument he had pressed since the Toy Biz years — that a successful film sells every other product the company makes — and it exposed the flaw in the licensing model at the same time, since Marvel's share of a gross above eight hundred million dollars was reported as a small fraction of it.

The film simplified the premise to its core — people born different, feared by the public — and drew heavily on Claremont's version of the characters. Its success, following Blade, demonstrated that superhero films could be made seriously for a general audience, and effectively started the current cycle.

Sam Raimi's film retold the Lee and Ditko origin closely, took a then-record opening weekend and grossed over eight hundred million dollars worldwide. Marvel, as licensor, received a fraction of that — the clearest demonstration of what the company was giving away.

The licensing income and the merchandise sales that followed the film were central to Marvel's recovery from bankruptcy, and the gap between what the film earned and what Marvel received was the argument that persuaded the company to borrow against its characters and produce its own films.

A second-tier character was chosen because his rights were among those Marvel still controlled and could borrow against. Jon Favreau's film, with Robert Downey Jr. in a role few would have predicted, made him one of the company's best-known characters within a decade.

The first film Marvel produced itself, financed against the rights to a group of characters and distributed by Paramount. A scene after the credits announcing a wider initiative told the audience that these films would share a continuity — the same device the comics had used since 1961.

The studio was set up in 1993 and spent its first decade licensing characters to others. From 2008 it produced the films itself, and built the shared continuity that became the highest-grossing franchise in cinema.

Feige joined as an assistant in 2000 and became president in 2007, having argued that the value of Marvel's library lay in the shared continuity rather than in any single character. He has overseen every film in the series and, since 2019, holds authority across Marvel's film, television and publishing output.

The 2012 film brought together characters introduced across five previous releases, executing in cinema the crossover structure Marvel's comics had used for fifty years. Its commercial scale established the model that the rest of the industry then attempted to copy, mostly without success.

Starlin's 1991 crossover supplied the spine of the two Avengers films that closed the series' first long arc: the gems, the glove, and the erasure of half of all life. The films rewrote Thanos's motive from courting Death to a doctrine about resources, but the structure is his.

The films took the character's wartime origin from Simon and Kirby and his modern arc from Brubaker's Winter Soldier and Millar's Civil War, keeping the central device intact: a man from 1945 measuring the present against what he was told he was fighting for.

The 2018 film drew on the Kirby conception of Wakanda and on the political framing that Christopher Priest and Ta-Nehisi Coates had developed, and became one of the highest-grossing films ever released in the United States — evidence of an audience the industry had long assumed did not exist for this material.
Kamala Khan reached television and film within a decade of her first appearance, a speed unmatched by any comparable Marvel character and a sign of how directly publishing now feeds the screen.

The character's film series began at Fox in 2016 and moved to Marvel Studios after Disney acquired the studio, carrying over the self-aware comedy that later writers, rather than his creators, had given him.
Starlin's character became the films' central antagonist across a decade of releases, with his motive rewritten from courting Death to a doctrine about overpopulation and resources.

Disney acquired Marvel Entertainment in a deal announced in August 2009 and completed that December, valued at around four billion dollars — a figure that looked large at the time and modest within a decade. The purchase gave Disney a library of characters with an audience its own brands reached less easily.

The 2009 acquisition brought Marvel's film production in-house and supplied the capital for a release schedule no independent studio could have financed. Disney's 2019 purchase of 21st Century Fox then returned the X-Men and Fantastic Four rights.

The films reversed the direction of influence. Comics were increasingly published to support characters the films had made famous, costume designs and casting fed back into the pages, and the publishing arm — the original business — became a comparatively small part of the company's revenue while remaining the source of everything it sells.

Lee appeared briefly in most Marvel films until his death in 2018, a running device that made him the visible link between the films and their origin. He had also litigated against Marvel over a share of film profits in 2002, settling in 2005.

Lee's own position in the argument is unusual: as editor he administered the work-for-hire terms his collaborators objected to, and as a salaried employee he received no ownership either, suing Marvel in 2002 over a share of film revenues and settling in 2005.

Lee sold his WildStorm studio to DC in a deal agreed in 1998 and effective from January 1999, joined the company as an artist, and rose to publisher and then president and chief creative officer — an unusual trajectory from Marvel's best-selling artist to the head of its principal competitor.
Starlin's cosmic work is the period's other direction: superhero comics used for metaphysics, mortality and self-annihilation, at a length and seriousness the Silver Age format had not attempted.
Conway's Spider-Man work marks the period's turn towards consequences that are not undone: the death of Gwen Stacy in 1973 is usually cited as the Bronze Age's founding event.

Miller's Daredevil and the adult-oriented work that followed it were viable because the direct market let publishers sell to a self-selecting audience through specialist shops, without newsstand distributors or the assumption of a child readership.

Marvel moved decisively into the direct market under Jim Shooter, launching titles sold only through comic shops. The system gave the company predictable orders and a committed readership, at the cost of the newsstand audience it never recovered.

The event format depends on the direct market: a crossover only lifts sales across a line if retailers order the tie-ins in advance and readers can reliably find every part of it, neither of which the newsstand could provide.

The company as it now exists dates from this period: the characters, the shared continuity, the editorial voice and the working method were all established between 1961 and 1966, and everything since has been built on or against them.

What separated Marvel's version of the revival from DC's was that its heroes were given ordinary problems — money, illness, unpopularity, each other — and a single New York they all occupied, so that a character could appear in someone else's book and the reader was expected to notice. Both devices are still the basis of the publishing line and of the films.

The Hulk was a founding member in 1963 and left in the second issue, unable to work with the others — an early signal that Marvel's teams would be held together by friction rather than by common purpose.
Thor was a founding member, and the team has repeatedly used him to raise the scale of its threats: a god on the roster makes cosmic-level opposition plausible in a book otherwise set in New York.

A founding member whose money and technology have generally underwritten the team, an arrangement later writers used to raise the question of who is accountable for a private army with a corporate sponsor.

Captain America was revived in The Avengers #4 in 1964, found frozen after twenty years, and made the team's leader. Bringing a Golden Age character forward gave Marvel's new universe a history and tied Timely's wartime output to the line Lee and Kirby were building.

Bendis put Luke Cage on the team in 2005, moving a street-level character created in the blaxploitation era into the company's flagship title and making his refusal to work for the government a running thread.
Namor joined the team in the 1980s, four decades after his creation and having spent most of that time as an antagonist — a case of Marvel's habit of resolving old rivalries by absorption.

Spider-Man was kept off the team for four decades on the grounds that he worked alone, and Bendis added him in 2005 as part of the deliberate reorientation of the title around Marvel's most popular characters.

The two characters fought across several issues in 1940 in one of the earliest crossovers in American comics, an extended battle through New York that established both that Timely's characters shared a world and that neither of them was straightforwardly heroic.

Feige has been the producer in charge of every film in the series, and the shared continuity is his structural decision rather than an inheritance: the studio's early releases were made to connect before there was evidence audiences wanted them to.

He imported from the comics both the crossover device and the practice of running a long arc over years, planning the slate in phases building to a common conclusion. Since 2019 he has also held authority over Marvel's television and publishing output, concentrating creative control over the characters in one office for the first time.

Simon and Kirby left Timely in 1941 in a dispute over promised profit-sharing on Captain America and went straight to National, where they worked on Sandman and the Boy Commandos. The first great creative partnership in comics moved between the two companies before either had settled into the rivalry that followed.

After walking out of Marvel in 1966 Ditko worked extensively at Charlton, where the rates were the lowest in the business and the editorial interference close to none. There he created the Question and revived Blue Beetle — the characters DC bought in 1983 and Alan Moore then asked to use.

Moore's original Watchmen proposal used the Charlton heroes DC had just acquired, and Rorschach is a direct reworking of Ditko's the Question: the absolutist with a blank face, whose objectivist certainty Moore kept and then examined until it broke. Ditko had no involvement in and no regard for the result.

Giordano moved from Charlton to DC in 1968 and brought several of its younger creators with him, including Denny O'Neil. The transfer of a small publisher's talent into the larger one supplied much of DC's Bronze Age staff, and Giordano himself returned later to run its editorial for a decade.

DC hired Byrne away from Marvel in 1986, at the height of his Fantastic Four run, to restart Superman after Crisis on Infinite Earths. Poaching a rival's most bankable writer-artist to rebuild your oldest character was a statement about how the competition then stood.

Wolfman left Marvel after his spell as editor-in-chief and found at DC the work he is best known for: The New Teen Titans, which became that company's best-selling title, and then Crisis on Infinite Earths. The move is the clearest single case of a creator's most important work happening on the other side of the rivalry.

Harras ran Marvel's editorial through bankruptcy and the loss of its star artists, left in 2000, and became DC's editor-in-chief in 2010 — holding the top editorial job at both companies, and presiding at DC over the New 52 relaunch.

Alonso edited at Vertigo under Karen Berger, working on Preacher and 100 Bullets, before moving to Marvel and eventually to its editor-in-chief's chair. The imprint functioned for years as a training ground whose alumni turned up throughout the other company's editorial.

After his break with DC's main line, Moore returned through WildStorm, writing WildC.A.T.s and then the America's Best Comics imprint — Promethea, Top 10, Tom Strong — under an arrangement he understood to be at arm's length from DC. DC's purchase of WildStorm placed him back inside the company he had left.

Morrison wrote New X-Men from 2001, stripping the costumes back to institutional uniforms, treating mutation as a demographic fact rather than a persecution metaphor, and pushing the school towards being a real school. It is the most substantial DC-associated writer's run at Marvel, and much of it was quietly reversed after they left.

Before The Ultimates, Millar wrote The Authority at WildStorm, taking Warren Ellis's premise of superheroes who intervene in world politics and pushing it to the point where DC's management intervened in the scripts. The template — widescreen action, heroes as a geopolitical force — is what he then took to Marvel.

Bendis left Marvel for DC in 2018 after nearly two decades as its most prolific writer, in one of the highest-profile exclusive-contract moves the industry has seen, and took over the Superman titles. The traffic that had run from DC to Marvel in the 1980s was by then running both ways.

Bendis took over Superman and Action Comics on arriving at DC in 2018, revealed Clark Kent's identity to the world, and introduced the Daily Planet to genuine competition — decisions of a kind he had spent the previous decade making at the other company.

Jim Starlin has said his first version of Thanos was closer to Kirby's Metron, and that Roy Thomas told him to make the character more imposing — more like Darkseid. Kirby's villain, created at DC after he left Marvel, therefore shaped Marvel's principal cosmic antagonist at second hand.

Kirby had been developing an ending for Marvel's Asgard — a Ragnarok that would clear the gods away and leave successors — when he left the company. He took the shape of it to DC and built the Fourth World from it, which is why the New Gods read as a second, unencumbered attempt at the material he had been drawing in Thor.

Marvel's Secret Wars reached print in 1984, a year before Crisis, and the two series between them established the line-wide crossover as a fixture of mainstream publishing. Their methods differed — a toy-driven battle planet against a continuity demolition — but both proved that an event running through every title would lift the whole line.

DC's 1992 storyline is the boom's other defining artefact alongside X-Men #1: black polybags, a memorial armband, worldwide news coverage, and enormous numbers of speculative buyers who never returned. Both companies were selling the same thing that year — the issue as investment rather than as reading.

DC took less structural damage than Marvel when the market collapsed, having neither bought a distributor nor borrowed against future sales, but it lost the speculative readership just as completely and spent the rest of the decade with a shrinking direct-market base.

Prestige-format work sold at a premium price to adults depended entirely on specialist shops: non-returnable orders let DC print for a known audience rather than gamble on newsstand sell-through. The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen are what the system made possible at DC, as Epic and the graphic-novel line were at Marvel.

An imprint publishing horror and literary comics without the Code seal could exist only where retailers knew their customers and ordered accordingly. Vertigo is the direct market's most complete vindication, and later its casualty, as the audience moved to bookshop collections.

The argument begins with Superman: sold outright for 130 dollars in 1938, litigated over for four decades, and settled only in 1975 by public pressure rather than by law. Every later campaign at either company — Simon's, Gerber's, Kirby's — was fought against the precedent that case set.

Moore understood Watchmen's rights to revert once the book went out of print; it never has. His refusal of credit and payment for adaptations, and his break with DC, made him the most visible modern example of the same complaint Kirby and Simon had pursued through the courts.

Kahn is the rare figure on the management side of the argument: she restored Siegel and Shuster's credit and pensions from inside Warner, then introduced royalties and creator incentives at DC in the same years Jim Shooter was doing so at Marvel, largely because both companies were losing talent over it.

WildStorm was Jim Lee's studio within Image, one of the founder-run imprints under the shared banner. When Lee sold it to DC the arrangement ended, moving a company founded on creator ownership into the ownership of one of the two publishers it had been founded against.

DC spent the 2010s attempting to assemble a shared film continuity on the Marvel model and failing to sequence it, and DC Studios was created in 2022 to impose the single planned continuity that Marvel had run since 2008. The device both were copying was the one the comics had used since Fantastic Four #1.
